certified_recipient_set.why: A rotator wraps to the certified set, never to the epoch roster. The roster enumerates every credential the service admitted; the certified set names the exact (credential_id ‖ W_pub ‖ S_pub) member triples a person enrolled, and the exact recovery recipient. Without it, account authorization alone causes delayed content-key delivery: at the next unrelated rotation nothing distinguishes an admitted credential from one whose ceremony succeeded.
certified_recipient_set.message: CertifiedSet = LP("done/certified-set/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec parent_epoch) || LP(dec next_epoch) || LP(hex members_digest) || LP(hex recovery_state_digest)
certified_recipient_set.members_digest: SHA-256( LP("done/certified-members/v1") || ( LP(credential_id) || LP(hex W_pub) || LP(hex S_pub) )* sorted by credential_id )
certified_recipient_set.approval_message: approval = Ed25519( the named approver’s signing credential ; LP("done/certified-set-approval/v1") || LP(approver_credential_id) || CertifiedSet )
certified_recipient_set.approved_by: One eligible content-holding client (P-1, single-owner). approvals[] is a list of (approver_credential_id, approval) entries, so a threshold is later a verifier policy change rather than a format migration.
certified_recipient_set.approver_resolution: The verifier resolves the named approver’s S_pub from the PARENT certified set’s member entry and nothing else — the genesis set under the creating credential’s key, a bootstrap-minted replacement under the factor-resolved signer. The service-signed epoch resolves no recipient-authority key (P-1, ratified 2026-08-28).
certified_recipient_set.expected: licensed_recipients equals wrapped_by_this_rotation, and admitted_but_uncertified appears in roster and in neither

bootstrap_composition.why: P-1 falsifier 17, run: an accepted RecoveryBootstrap’s binding IS the replacement certified set, and a subsequent rotation by the recovered credential succeeds — its approval resolving through the replacement set’s member entry, the same lookup every approval uses. Round 1 D-3 found this composed nowhere: the recovered credential could read and could not rotate.
bootstrap_composition.rule: replacement set = one member entry (new_credential_id ‖ new_W_pub ‖ new_S_pub) with new_recovery_state_digest, at parent_epoch = observed_epoch, verifying under the factor-resolved bootstrap signer (TRD §13.8, S0-2/A-schemas.md §2)
bootstrap_composition.consumes: test/vectors/head-discovery.json recovery_bootstrap.fields — the composition is by value, not by a second copy of the story

subsequent_rotation.resolved_through: the replacement set’s member entry — resolveApprover(replacement_members, approver)

bootstrap_composition.expected: the recovered credential’s successor approval verifies through the replacement set

construction.one_protocol: One intent-and-outcome protocol at three kinds -- rotate, replace-recovery, retire -- because §11.2 test 11s list is one class: a multi-step transition whose interrupted middle can be mistaken for a completed *lesser* transition.
construction.intent: Intent = LP("done/transition/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(kind) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec parent_epoch) || LP(dec target) || LP(hex payload_digest), signed by the requesting device credential. id = SHA-256(Intent).
construction.outcome: Outcome = LP("done/transition-out/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(kind) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec target) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex committed_id), signed by the lineage authorization key.
construction.kind_binding: PRD §6.10s "deliberate downgrade must not silently become account deletion" is a binding requirement rather than an interface one. rotate and retire are otherwise the same eight fields, and an unbound kind is a way to submit one and commit the other. Row 3s editable-kind finding at a third object.
construction.lapse_is_not_a_kind: What the binding above closes is the rotate/retire pair, and not lapse (S0-7). No field of a rotation expresses a payment lapse, a synchronization stop or a retention deadline, so binding kind cannot protect a state this grammar has no way to say. TRD §14.7 carries it, on a second axis, under a signer that is not the lineage authorization key. scripts/check-retention.mjs enforces that the two vocabularies stay disjoint.
construction.no_from_gen: There is no from_gen field. §13.5s epoch binds the current content-key generation, so the generation being rotated from is a function of parent_epoch. Row 10 left out a part count and row 12 an algorithm field on the same rule: a second binding of a derivable fact is a thing that can disagree with it.
construction.idempotency: The service commits at most one intent per (lineage_id, kind, target). A retry is the same bytes: the payload digest sorts its parts, so rebuilding from inputs in a different order reproduces the id exactly.
construction.three_way_rule: Silence: wait, then resubmit the identical bytes. Outcome with committed_id == id: committed, apply. Outcome with committed_id != id: superseded, discard and rebuild against the new epoch -- never resubmit, because the exclusion set was computed against an epoch that has moved. Everything that is not a verified outcome is silence.
construction.authenticated_refusal: Row 6 established that a definite refusal licenses a re-mint and silence does not, and did not say the refusal must be authenticated. Here it must: the third case discards a live content key, and anything that can withhold an outcome can fabricate one.
construction.no_state_field: Whether you won is committed_id == your id. A state flag would be a second binding of the same fact that could disagree with it, and an implementation reading the flag rather than comparing would discard a live key. Row 10s rule about the part count.
construction.no_nonce: (lineage, kind, target) names an immutable pair, so an outcome re-served forever is the truth rather than a replay. The contrast with row 9s head assertion, which needed a nonce because a head moves.
construction.local_order: The pending intent is persisted before the first network byte. No content is written under the target generation before a verified committed outcome, and none under the previous generation after it -- the commit is one transition point and neither half may precede it. On restart a pending intent is resubmitted, never rebuilt.
construction.retention: The previous generation is retained until the outcome is committed, a checkpoint under the new generation is admitted (row 7), and the local trim holds a state record under it (§6.1). Dropping on fewer than three is the failure found at a restore rather than at a review.
construction.length_prefix: uint16be(byteLength) || utf8 -- injective, so no field can shift another.

authorization.role: The lineage's authorization key (§13.5). Signs epochs, and signs the outcome that settles a transition.

owner.role: The rotating device's signing credential (§13.4). Produces the intent; §13.7 forbids the service producing the key.

impostor.role: Neither. A relay that can withhold can also fabricate, and a fabricated refusal is what this row has to refuse.

intent_vectors.name: rotate
intent_vectors.why: The row's central case: a fresh generation, its wraps, the excluded credential and row 5s cutoff. Persisted before the first network byte, which is what makes the crash resolvable rather than ambiguous.

intent_vectors.name: retire
intent_vectors.why: Account deletion (§14.4). **Identical to the rotate above in every field but `kind` and its payload**, which is why PRD §6.10s warning is a binding requirement rather than an interface one.

intent_vectors.name: replace-recovery
intent_vectors.why: The atomic replace §13.8 requires and row 14 §5 handed to this review. Same shape: an interruption must leave exactly the old envelope or exactly the new, because two live recovery envelopes means the old code still opens content.

outcome_vectors.name: rotate--committed
outcome_vectors.why: The settlement that licenses applying the transition. Signed by the lineage authorization key, because discarding or applying a content key on the strength of an unsigned answer is what this row refuses.

outcome_vectors.name: retire--committed
outcome_vectors.why: The settlement that licenses applying the transition. Signed by the lineage authorization key, because discarding or applying a content key on the strength of an unsigned answer is what this row refuses.

outcome_vectors.name: replace-recovery--committed
outcome_vectors.why: The settlement that licenses applying the transition. Signed by the lineage authorization key, because discarding or applying a content key on the strength of an unsigned answer is what this row refuses.

outcome_vectors.name: rotate--superseded
outcome_vectors.why: The third case, and the one that only exists because a transition carries an exclusion set. Another owner device rotated to the same generation first and excluded a *different* credential. The loser must not resubmit -- its exclusion set was computed against an epoch that has moved -- so this is the one answer that licenses discarding a live key, and the one an attacker would forge.

inputs.note: The rival intent differs from ours only in its excluded set, which is why its id differs and its payload digest is published beside it.

demonstrations.name: an-outcome-re-served-is-not-a-replay
demonstrations.why: Row 9's head assertion needed a nonce because a head is a statement about a moving lineage, so re-serving one is a replay. `(lineage, kind, target)` names an immutable pair -- generations are monotone and a target is reached once -- so this statement does not go stale and there is nothing to bind freshness to. Verifying the same outcome a second time yields the same verdict, deliberately.

demonstrations.name: a-retry-is-the-same-bytes
demonstrations.why: The idempotency key is SHA-256 of the intent message, and the payload digest sorts its parts, so rebuilding the intent from inputs in a different order reproduces it exactly. That is what makes "resubmit on silence" safe: the resubmission cannot accidentally be a second, different transition.

demonstrations.name: a-replacement-is-bound-to-its-exact-bytes
demonstrations.why: Row 14 offers replacement as the answer to a lost -- or exposed -- code, and row 15 says an interruption leaves exactly the old envelope or exactly the new. Both sentences are claims about bytes. The superseded payload bound the new public key and the string "1|2|3|4|5", so it said which generations were rewrapped and never to what: each variant below is a complete, well-formed replacement differing from the selected one in one place, and the first three collided with it. Published as digests rather than asserted in prose, because the collision is the whole finding.

superseded_construction.note: What the first three variants above could not be distinguished from.

demonstrations.expected: every variant differs from the selected digest

demonstrations.name: a-rotation-and-a-retirement-differ-in-one-field
demonstrations.why: PRD §6.10 says a deliberate downgrade must not silently become account deletion. These two intents are the same workspace, lineage, parent epoch and target; the messages diverge at `kind` and again at the payload it selects. Published side by side because the sentence reads as interface guidance and is a binding requirement.
demonstrations.expected: neither message opens as the other

must_fail.name: certified-set-approved-by-an-impostor
must_fail.why: The approval is the whole difference between a roster and a recipient set, and this is round 1's mutation inverted into the permanent shape of the negative (P-1 falsifier 12): the verifier resolves the named approver's S_pub from the parent certified set's member entry — a real lookup, not a constant — so a hostile service that publishes an epoch substituting a member's signing key gets an approval that does not verify. The epoch certifies no recipient-authority key, and the verifier never asks it.

must_fail.name: approval-presented-as-another-members
must_fail.why: P-1 falsifier 13: the approver is named inside the approval's signed bytes, so presenting one member's approval under another member's name changes the message the signature was taken over — flipping the name breaks the signature, and one eligible member cannot replay another's approval as its own.

must_fail.name: approval-without-a-named-approver
must_fail.why: The pre-return approval shape — a signature over the bare set bytes, naming nobody — is malformed by construction: the verifier only accepts the labeled, approver-prefixed message, so an approval that does not say who approved cannot verify under anyone.

must_fail.name: approval-by-an-admitted-non-member
must_fail.why: The eligibility rule as a lookup. The intruder is in the service's roster and not in the parent certified set, so an approval naming it refuses at resolution — before any signature runs. Admission is the service's to grant and approval authority is not: criterion 10's authorized-but-unkeyed credential stays outside, now for approvals as well as wraps.

must_fail.name: certified-set-from-another-epoch
must_fail.why: A set approved against one parent epoch, presented at a later one. Without the parent binding, an approval collected when a credential was legitimately a member survives its removal, and a rotator replays a stale membership as a current one.

must_fail.name: certified-set-with-an-added-member
must_fail.why: The row, as a signature check. The service adds a credential it admitted to the members and presents the honest approval beside it. The approval covers `members_digest`, so the added member changes the message the signature was taken over.

must_fail.name: certified-set-with-substituted-recovery-state
must_fail.why: The same at the recovery carrier: the approval covers `recovery_state_digest`, so a substituted R_pub cannot ride an honest approval. This is what stops a correctly-enrolled device wrapping future generations to a key the service holds.

must_fail.name: fabricated-refusal
must_fail.why: The attack row 6 left open. A definite refusal licenses discarding a live content key and rebuilding; silence does not. Row 6 stated the rule and did not say the refusal must be authenticated -- so anything that can withhold an outcome can fabricate one, and induce a rotation to be thrown away and rebuilt against an epoch of the attacker's choosing. Signed by a key that is not the lineage's authorization key.

must_fail.name: unsigned-outcome
must_fail.why: The same at its most ordinary: an error body with no signature at all. It is silence, and the client waits.

must_fail.name: outcome-from-an-older-epoch
must_fail.why: An outcome whose epoch is at or below the intent parent. It cannot be settling this intent, because the intent was built against that parent.

must_fail.name: flipped-signature-bit
must_fail.why: The signature doing its own job.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-label
must_fail.why: The domain-separation label, isolated. It is the whole of what stops a signed statement of another kind being read as a transition intent.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-version
must_fail.why: Row 1's rule: a carrier version selects the suite, so a renumbered intent must fail rather than select a weaker one.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-kind
must_fail.why: PRD §6.10 as bytes. A rotate and a retire are otherwise the same eight fields; unbound, `kind` is how a deliberate downgrade commits as an account deletion. Row 3's editable-`kind` finding at a third object.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-workspace-id
must_fail.why: An intent lifted between workspaces on one profile -- PRD §6.7s two-principal case, not an attack.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-lineage-id
must_fail.why: The lineage a migration replaces (§14.1). Unbound, a pre-migration intent could commit against the successor lineage, which is exactly what §14.2 forbids replaying.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-parent-epoch
must_fail.why: Which epoch the exclusion set was computed against. It is what makes a stale intent detectable rather than merely wrong.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-target
must_fail.why: The generation being rotated to, and half the idempotency key. Unbound, a retry could commit at a different generation than the one it was built for.

must_fail.name: aad-only-intent-payload-digest
must_fail.why: The wraps, the exclusion set and the cutoff. Unbound, the service commits an epoch whose excluded set is not the one the client signed -- a revocation that revokes someone else.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-label
must_fail.why: The same isolation for the outcome, and the two labels differ so an intent can never be presented as its own settlement.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-version
must_fail.why: The outcome carrier version, isolated from the intent version, because they are separate carriers.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-kind
must_fail.why: An outcome for a retire presented as the settlement of a rotate. The client would apply a generation switch on the strength of a signature over something else.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-workspace-id
must_fail.why: Another workspace's settlement on the same device.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-lineage-id
must_fail.why: The same across lineages, which is the migration boundary.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-target
must_fail.why: Which generation was settled. Unbound, an old settlement licenses discarding a key for a rotation still in flight.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-epoch
must_fail.why: Which epoch committed it. Isolated by using two epochs the same authorization key signs -- §13.5 rotates `K_accept` and not the authorization key, which is what makes the field varyable without varying the verifier.

must_fail.name: aad-only-outcome-committed-id
must_fail.why: The field the whole three-way rule turns on. Unbound, an attacker flips a commit into a supersede and the client discards a content key the service holds wraps for -- the interrupted state masquerading as a completed lesser one, which is this rows whole subject. The substituted id is another kinds intent rather than the rival rotations, because the rival differs in one field and eliding that field would rescue this negative for the wrong reason.

primitive_kats: Ed25519 and SHA-256 KATs are row 1's, in test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json. This generator checks that row 1 still selects Ed25519 for signatures, so the two documents fail apart rather than drift apart.
